children: Sri Lanka's central bank raised its key policy rate by 25 basis points in a surprise move on Friday, citing higher-than-expected inflation pressures caused by volatile global energy prices.
Markets had expected the Central Bank of Sri Lanka (CBSL) to stay put for a third consecutive meeting after an unexpected hike of 100 basis points in May.
The increase, which brings its overnight policy rate to 9%, underscores the island nation's vulnerability to gains in energy prices as it imports all of its fuel.
Sri Lanka has lifted fuel prices by about 35% this year. As a result, inflation has shot up from 2.2% in March to 8.3% last month.
The CBSL said in a statement that while global energy prices have eased recently, the impact of previous increases is expected to exert pressures on prices in the near term.

"Latest projections also showed that inflation could remain higher in the near term and for longer than previously projected, before returning to the target of 5% in the second half of 2027," the statement said.
"Inflation expectations, particularly in the one-year period ahead, have also risen recently, although medium-term inflation expectations remain anchored around the target," it said.
At 9%, the overnight policy rate is the highest it has been since the rate was introduced at 8% in November 2024.
The CBSL also increased the Statutory Reserve Ratio (SRR) rate by 100 basis points to 3% to mop up excess rupee liquidity in the market.

"This policy and SRR change shows the central bank’s focus is shifting to reserve building. It will have an impact on growth leading into next year," said Udeeshan Jonas, chief strategist at Capital Alliance.
Sri Lanka had $7.1 billion in reserves in October.
The central bank's move comes ahead of a review by the International Monetary Fund of its $2.9 billion program for the country.

The IMF will evaluate Sri Lanka's budget that was presented to parliament on November 12 and the central bank's latest policy decision as part of this review, its seventh. If the review goes well, Sri Lanka will receive $345 million — its second-last installment under the program.
Sri Lanka is still recovering from a deep financial crisis four years ago when foreign reserves ran dangerously low, leaving it unable to pay for fuel and other essentials.
Overnight policy rate hiked by 25 basis points to 9%
Central bank had been expected to stay put for third straight meeting
Reserve ratio also lifted by 100 basis points
